::: {.lead-box}
How are machine-learning methods used to **tune, model, monitor and control** particle
accelerators? This course gives a map of the main methods — what they are, what they need,
when to use them — and lets you try each of them on a simulated beamline, directly in your
browser.
:::

[▶ Open the slides](slides/ml4acc.qmd){.btn-slides}
[Exercises on Colab](exercises.qmd){.btn-slides .secondary}

## Audience and prerequisites

Students and young researchers in accelerator physics with **no prior machine-learning
background**. You need basic Python and the basics of transverse beam optics (drifts,
quadrupoles, beam size). Nothing to install: the exercises run on Google Colab.

## Course outline (60 min)

| Time | Part | Content |
|:--|:--|:--|
| 0–8 min | Why ML for accelerators? | many knobs, noise, drifts, costly simulations; the four families of tasks |
| 8–25 min | Machine learning from scratch | supervised / unsupervised / reinforcement learning; data, model, loss; gradient descent; neural networks step by step (neuron, activation, layers, backpropagation); overfitting and test sets |
| 25–52 min | A tour of the methods | surrogate models & virtual diagnostics · Bayesian optimisation · anomaly detection & fault classification · reinforcement learning · differentiable simulations |
| 52–58 min | Good practice | evaluation, uncertainty, safety; take-home messages |

## Hands-on exercises

Four notebooks, all built on the same three-quadrupole beamline simulated with
[Cheetah](https://github.com/desy-ml/cheetah), a fast and differentiable beam-dynamics code
written in PyTorch. See the [exercises page](exercises.qmd).
